lead: The laws of mechanics are written for a fixed mass of fluid. A pipe, a nozzle or a pump casing is easier to draw as a fixed region in space. The Reynolds transport theorem joins the two views: it turns the rate of change of a property of a fixed mass into a rate of change inside a chosen region plus the net rate carried out across its boundary. Mass, momentum, angular momentum and energy conservation all fall out of it by choosing one property. Pump design, jet impact on a Pelton bucket and the force on a pipe bend all rest on it.
prereq: You need Unit 2: the system and control volume distinction, the continuity equation, and streamlines.

sections.h3: System, control volume, and the bridge between them

blocks.text: A system is a fixed mass of fluid — a named set of particles that we follow. It moves, stretches and changes shape, but no mass crosses its boundary. Newton's second law, d(mV)/dt = ΣF, is written for exactly this kind of body.

A control volume is a fixed region in space. Its boundary is the control surface, drawn once and left in place. Fluid enters and leaves through it. A pipe section, a nozzle, a pump casing, the gap between two turbine blades — all are drawn this way, because a fixed region is easy to mark on a drawing and easy to instrument.

The difficulty: physics speaks about the system, the geometry speaks about the control volume. The Reynolds transport theorem is the bridge. It says the rate of change of a property of the system equals the rate of change of that property inside the control volume plus the net rate at which the property is carried out across the control surface.

Two words before the formula. An extensive property B grows with the amount of fluid present: mass, momentum, energy. Its intensive value is b = B/m, the same property per kilogram. With density ρ in kg/m³, the amount of B inside a small volume dV is ρb dV.
Take any control volume that coincides with the system at the instant considered. Then:

blocks.where: B is the extensive property of the system (kg, kg·m/s, J); b = B/m is that property per unit mass; ρ is density in kg/m³; V is the fluid velocity vector in m/s; n is the unit normal to the control surface, pointing outward from the control volume; dV is a volume element in m³ and dA an area element in m². The first integral runs over the control volume, the second over its surface.

blocks.text: First term, the storage term: how fast the amount of B inside the region is growing. It is a partial derivative because the region is fixed while ρ and b may change with time at each point.

Second term, the flux term: ρb is the amount of B per unit volume, V·n is the volume leaving per unit area per second, so the product integrated over the surface is the net rate at which B is carried out. Where flow leaves, V·n is positive. Where flow enters, V·n is negative, so an inflow subtracts.
At the chosen instant the control surface and the system boundary are the same surface, so both sides describe the same fluid.

sections.h3: Steady form and the four special cases

blocks.text: For steady flow nothing inside changes with time and the storage term vanishes:
dB/dt = Σ ρ b (V·n) A,  and with one inlet 1 and one outlet 2:  dB/dt = ṁ(b₂ − b₁)
blocks.where: ṁ = ρQ is the mass flow rate in kg/s, Q is discharge in m³/s, A is the area of a section in m², and b₁, b₂ are the values of b at inlet and outlet.

items: Put b = 1: B is mass, dB/dt = 0, so ṁ₂ = ṁ₁. This is the continuity equation.
Put b = V: B is momentum, dB/dt = ΣF, the force on the fluid. Worked out in 3.6.
Put b = r × V, where r is the position vector from a chosen point: B is angular momentum and the result gives torque about that point.
Put b = e = u + V²/2 + gz, where u is internal energy per kg, V²/2 kinetic energy per kg and gz potential energy per kg: B is energy.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call it the Reynolds transport equation, or present it as Leibniz's rule applied to a volume whose boundary moves with the fluid. If the control volume itself moves or deforms, replace V by the relative velocity W = V − Vcv inside the surface integral. Shrinking the control volume to a thin streamtube gives Euler's equation.

figure.caption: The rate of change of a system property splits into what happens inside the region and what crosses its boundary; adding the two gives the theorem.

spec.title: From system to control volume
spec.aria: A block diagram splitting the rate of change of a system property into an inside-the-control-volume term and a net outward flux term, which together form the Reynolds transport theorem.

examples.question: Water (density 1000 kg/m³) flows steadily through a fixed control volume. At inlet section 1 the area is 0.01 m² and the velocity is 2 m/s. At outlet section 2 the area is 0.02 m². Find the discharge, the outlet velocity, the net rate at which momentum leaves the control volume, and the force acting on the fluid.
steps: Discharge from the inlet: Q = A₁V₁ = 0.01 × 2 = 0.02 m³/s.
Continuity for steady flow gives V₂ = Q/A₂ = 0.02 / 0.02 = 1 m/s.
Flow is steady, so the storage term ∂/∂t ∫ρb dV is zero and only the surface flux survives.
Take b = V and the outward normal at each section. Momentum flux out = ρQ(V₂ − V₁) = 1000 × 0.02 × (1 − 2) = −20 N.
The negative sign means the net momentum flux is directed upstream; equivalently, 20 N of momentum per second leaves in the negative direction.
From the momentum form, ΣF on the fluid = momentum out − momentum in = −20 N, so the force on the fluid is 20 N pointing upstream, that is against the flow direction.
examples.answer: Q = 0.02 m³/s, V₂ = 1 m/s, net momentum flux = −20 N (20 N upstream), and the force on the fluid is 20 N acting upstream.
examples.check:
A1 = 0.01
V1 = 2.0
A2 = 0.02
rho = 1000.0
Q = A1 * V1
V2 = Q / A2
mom_flux = rho * Q * (V2 - V1)
force_on_fluid = -mom_flux
print(Q)
print(V2)
print(mom_flux)
print(force_on_fluid)

traps: Using the acceleration of the system in place of the surface flux integral. The theorem needs ρb(V·n) integrated over the surface, not a material derivative written at a point.
Forgetting that n points outward. An inlet gives V·n < 0, so inflow enters the sum with a minus sign; the commonest sign error in the unit.
Applying the steady form while the amount inside the control volume is changing, as in a tank being filled or a surge travelling down a pipe.
Mixing up B and b. Using momentum in kg·m/s where the per-unit-mass value V in m/s was needed, or the reverse, throws the answer off by a factor of ṁ.
Writing the storage derivative as a total derivative. Inside a fixed region ρ and b vary with position as well as time, so it must be ∂/∂t.

quiz.q: Define a system and a control volume in fluid mechanics.
quiz.a: A system is a fixed identified mass of fluid that moves and deforms with the flow; no mass crosses its boundary. A control volume is a fixed region in space with a boundary called the control surface, through which fluid may enter and leave.

quiz.q: In the surface integral ∫ρb(V·n)dA, why does n point outward, and what sign results at an inlet?
quiz.a: Pointing n outward makes the integral a net outflow. At an inlet the velocity opposes n, so V·n is negative and that section subtracts from the sum.

quiz.q: Newton's second law is written for a fixed mass. Why can it not be applied directly to the water in a pipe bend?
quiz.a: The water in the bend is not a fixed mass; different particles are in the bend at different times. The theorem converts the fixed-mass statement into storage inside the bend plus flux through its two sections, which are measurable quantities.

quiz.q: Write the steady-flow form of the theorem for one inlet and one outlet, and state what b is for mass conservation.
quiz.a: dB/dt = ṁ(b₂ − b₁) with ṁ = ρQ. For mass, B = m and b = 1, so dB/dt = 0 and ṁ₂ = ṁ₁, which is continuity.

quiz.q: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ enters a steady control volume at section 1 with A₁ = 0.005 m² and V₁ = 3 m/s, and leaves at section 2 with A₂ = 0.015 m². Find V₂ and the net rate of momentum leaving.
quiz.a: Q = A₁V₁ = 0.005 × 3 = 0.015 m³/s. V₂ = Q/A₂ = 0.015/0.015 = 1 m/s. Momentum flux out = ρQ(V₂ − V₁) = 1000 × 0.015 × (1 − 3) = −30 N, that is 30 N of momentum per second leaving upstream.

quiz.q: A tank is being filled from a pipe while water also drains from a hole in the bottom. Explain which terms of the theorem are non-zero and what happens if the steady form is used.
quiz.a: The control volume is the tank. The storage term ∂/∂t ∫ρb dV is non-zero because the mass and momentum inside grow or shrink with time. The surface terms are the inflow and the outflow. Setting the storage term to zero would wrongly force inflow equal to outflow, so it would predict a fixed water level and miss the filling or emptying altogether.

quiz.q: A control volume is drawn around the rotor of a centrifugal pump and rotates with it. How must the theorem be modified and why?
quiz.a: The surface of the control volume is moving, so the outward flux uses the velocity of the fluid relative to the surface, W = V − V<sub>cv</sub>, in place of V. The storage term is unchanged in form because it is evaluated at the same instant in a fixed frame. With this replacement, b = r × V gives the torque transmitted to the fluid, as used in Unit 7 for pump work.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same theorem, written for a control volume that shrinks to a point, produces the differential conservation laws used in computational fluid dynamics, where the equations are integrated over millions of small cells. Weather models, aircraft aerodynamics and blood-flow simulation all run on that discrete form. Industrial pipe-network software applies the steady form node by node to find flows and pressures. Renewable-energy work on tidal turbines uses the moving-control-volume form to get torque. Search next for the general transport equation, the finite volume method, and the Leibniz rule for a moving region.
